nonCandidates.site: packages/agent-engine/src/domain.ts:490-496 (quiet → `unsigned`) and :152 (NUDGE). Closest to a candidate: "did this session finish and merely forget to sign off?"
nonCandidates.why:
This is the only semantic read in the engine. I rejected it on its numbers.

Store counts, ~/.agent-workflows/engine/tasks, 453 journals:
- 314 are agent tasks and 305 of those carry a closeoutSchema.
- 0 attempts ended `reason: unsigned`.
- 0 `starting` events carry a `nudge`.
- 450 ended events: 449 `harness`, 1 `lost`.

Schema'd tasks that ended with no closeout: 5 of 305 (1.6%). They are v27t-implement and its try2 on 09-13, then 4ifo-implement, 3xq9-implement and vjcj-implement-try2 on 09-17.

The three after the unsigned fix (c7ed37f, 09-14) all ended `observed: done, reason: harness` and settled `succeeded`. The registry listed them done, not quiet. That is the "second door" open-issues.md:729-732 predicted and had not measured. So the engine's nudge never fired. A person's `wf retry --message` closed each one: the next try was filed 2 to 22 minutes later, ran 25 to 43 seconds over 3 to 4 turns, and cost $0.66, $0.82 and $0.93.

I sampled the final prose of all three transcripts. Each says it is done in plain words: "The work is complete and the check is green. Signing off."; "The workflow builder is done: … passed from the root"; "The web app now runs on … nothing uncommitted".

Why Jev is not the fix:
1. No consumer would branch on the answer. NUDGE already covers both cases in one sentence ("the work stands … If the work is not finished, finish it first"), so "finished or stopped midway" changes nothing the code does.
2. The real defect is plain code. A `done` sighting with a schema and no closeout should end `unsigned`, as quiet does, and the workflow layer files `maxAttempts: 1`, so no nudged attempt is available. Fixing those removes the person's minutes with no model involved.
3. Synthesising a closeout from the prose to skip the ~$0.80 resume would save about $4 across 305 tasks. It would also replace the session's own typed statement with a model's reading of self-advocating text from an agent with a stake, which the Jev docs name as an input that can steer its answer.
4. "The engine is finished" (CLAUDE.md:148). A model call here would be a callback into judgement.

candidates.evidence: I read every closeout in ~/.agent-workflows/engine/tasks/*.jsonl against runs/*.json. 65 runs have a review, and 43 of them looped at least once (30 with two reviews, 13 with three). 56 reviews said `again: true`, and every one carried findings. One of the 56 rounds had all its findings in .md files (close-the-fence-ahlx). A round is a resumed implement session plus a fresh review. The implement session cost a median of $8.07 (32 measured, $304.76 in total) and the review about $3-8, so a round is roughly $12 and the 56 rounds roughly $670. The implementer's replies read 144 `fixed` against 7 `won't fix`. I read 14 round-2 findings that asked for a third round, and all 14 were concrete behaviour bugs, none nits. So on this evidence the loop is mostly earning its rounds.
candidates.judgment: For each finding of a review that said `again: true`: "Does this finding describe a concrete input or case that produces a wrong result in shipped behaviour, rather than wording, documentation, naming or a test's style?"
candidates.options: P(yes) for each finding, asked in one fan-out request. For the round: `substantive` when any finding has P at or above the threshold, `nit-round` when all are below it, and `uncertain` when the confidence is low. `uncertain` is counted and never acted on.
candidates.state: One finding: `file`, `line`, and the `what` string from the reviewer's closeout (`ended.closeout.findings[]`). Nothing else: no diff and no implementer text. A review's findings are a median of about 375 tokens and at most about 1,460, so a finding is about 100-400 tokens and a whole review costs under $0.0001.
candidates.consumer: This is a measure only. It would add a line such as `round 2 was asked for on 0 of 3 substantive findings` to the `wf decide` screen and the misses arithmetic, and read from the record. It never overrides `again`, because a weaker reader that sees only the finding must not outvote an opus reviewer that read the code (workflow.ts:16-20). Low confidence means no line is printed.
candidates.whenAsked: Once, when a looping step's closeout with `again: true` is first seen. It is filed as its own engine task, as `checkTaskId` does for checks (runner.ts:485), with a deterministic task id per review try. Its journal would carry the question text, `jev-1.13.0`, the probabilities and the confidence. A later pass finds the settled task and never re-asks.
candidates.wrongCost: Nothing acts on the answer, so a wrong answer costs a misleading line on a screen that a person reads beside the findings themselves. If it were ever promoted to gating `again`, a wrong `nit` would ship a bug that the reviewer had found. That is why it should not be promoted.

If the measure showed that a tenth of rounds were nit rounds, that would be about 5 rounds or $60 over this store's history, and the fix would then be content (the review brief), not Jev. Its real worth is closing features.md:266 with a number. A cheaper first step is for the owner to hand-label the 56 rounds, which is about an hour and also yields the threshold data.

They are a weak label, since a nit can also be fixed. No person-made nit/substantive label exists. The roughly 150 findings across the 56 rounds would need labelling by hand.

verdicts.plainCode:
There are two options, and both are enough.

- **Hand-label once.** The owner labels the 148 findings in about an hour, as the survey itself suggests. That gives the number features.md:266 lacks. With nits this rare, a single count is what is needed, not a standing meter.
- **A `kind` enum per finding in review.schema.json.** If a standing signal is wanted, add something like `bug | untested-case | doc-the-next-run-reads | polish`. The opus reviewer that read the diff then writes the label into a typed closeout recorded once, for free. `wf misses` can count polish-only rounds by arithmetic.

The survey uses the second argument itself to reject the findings-triage site: "a schema field beats a second model wherever an agent already signs a typed closeout". It applies here unchanged. A self-label can be gamed, but so can the prose Jev would read, and the reviewer has more context than a reader of one finding.
verdicts.jaggedEdge:
Self-advocating state and literal reading.

- **Self-advocating state.** The finding text is the reviewer's own case for its round, and the schema requires it to be written as a concrete failure.
- **Literal reading.** "Documentation" and "wording" in the question match real defects in this repository's briefs and workflow folders.

Size is not a problem: a finding is a median of 840 characters and at most 1,975.
verdicts.ruleVerdict:
The placement keeps the letter of the rules. It would be asked once, as an engine task filed by runner.ts the way `checkTaskId` is at runner.ts:485. The answer would be journalled, displayed only, and would never touch `assess`. The engine would not change.

It breaks two reasons behind the rules:

- **A tool earns its place by replacing more code than it adds (CLAUDE.md).** This replaces none.
- **A model's reading on the `wf decide` screen (shape-tekton.md:181).** That document wants a miss to be "arithmetic over records — no model in the loop". A probability printed beside `again` is a third opinion with no standing, which is what README.md:1000-1002 warns against. It sits on the screen where a person commits to an answer.

check.ts:14-16's objection to marking your own homework also applies, in mirror image: the text being judged was written by the agent whose request is being judged.
verdicts.placement:
None, because it is rejected.

If the owner overrules this, the only shape that fits is the survey's:

- **Where:** a harness defined in agent-workflows and filed by runner.ts next to the check. It gets one deterministic task id per review try.
- **What it records:** the journal carries the question text, the pinned `jev-1.13.0`, the per-finding probability and the confidence.
- **How it is used:** it is read by `wf misses` only, never by `assess` and never printed on `wf decide`.
verdicts.probe:
This needs no build and no Jev, and it comes first in any case.

- **Dataset:** the 148 findings of the 56 `again: true` closeouts in ~/.agent-workflows/engine/tasks/*review*.jsonl.
- **Label:** the owner marks each finding as "worth a round" or "could have gone with again:false".
- **Metric:** the share of rounds where every finding is in the second class.
- **Bar:** if that share is under about 10% (5 or fewer rounds, roughly $60 over the store's history), close features.md:266 with the number and stop.

If it is higher, fix the brief and add the `kind` enum. A Jev probe would be worth running only if the labels turn up at least 30 nit findings. With fewer negatives no threshold can be tuned, and Jev's calibration claim holds across groups of predictions, not per answer. Offline, it would have to beat the reviewer's own `kind` label on those same findings.
verdicts.surveyWasWrong:
- **`stateAuthor: agent-without-a-stake` is wrong.** The reviewer writes `what` and `again` in the same closeout, and review.schema.json:12 makes every finding read as a concrete failure. The proposed question therefore has almost no negative class to find.
- **The nit definition is wrong for this store.** It counts a documentation finding as a nit. 15 of the 148 findings are on `.md` files, and the ones I read were defects in briefs, workflow steps or facts the next run reads.
- **"65 runs have a review" does not match the journals.** Their task names show 78 runs with a review task, and ~/.agent-workflows/runs holds 76 records. The 43 looped runs and 56 `again: true` closeouts do match. I count 148 findings where the survey says about 150.
- **The token figure for findings looks low.** The survey gives a median of about 375 tokens for a whole review's findings. I measure a median of 840 characters per finding, and a review carries 2 to 3 of them. It is still trivially cheap.
- **Cost and consistency.** The median cost of an `again: true` review is $3.80, at the low end of the survey's "$3-8". The survey also rejects findings-triage with the schema-field argument and does not apply the same argument to its own candidate.

challenge.layerVerdict: `packages/agent-workflows` is not a good home for Jev today. Its judgments already sit in typed closeouts signed by agents that read the code, and its facts are exit codes, files and git. Wherever a label is missing, a schema enum on the closeout gets it free from the better-informed reader, and the one surviving candidate measures a problem the store does not show. If a typed judgment ever enters this layer, it should be a journalled engine task like a check, asked once with the model version pinned. It should read only evidence no agent with a stake wrote, and nothing in the 453 journals offers that today.

synthesis.layerAnswer:
Jev does not belong in any layer as shipped machinery today. The only survivor is a trial, and it should be measured offline before anything is built.

- **`packages/agent-engine`: not a home.** Every decision in it is a structural read, a timing comparison or a declared policy field. "The engine is finished" and the pure `decide` exclude a model call there. Even the favourable frame, a judgment filed as a task, puts nothing in the engine. The `check` harness is a `HarnessSpec` value that agent-workflows hands to the engine (`/home/yrnd1/projects/hkb-v2/packages/agent-workflows/src/check.ts:117`). The engine would journal a Jev task with no change, and it should never depend on `@typesafe-ai/sdk`.
- **`packages/agent-workflows`: not a home today.** This is the layer the no-LLM rule protects: `assess`, `wf decide` and the misses arithmetic. Its judgments already sit in typed closeouts signed by agents that read the code, so a missing label is a schema enum, not a second model. If a typed judgment ever enters, this layer owns the mechanism, because `runner.ts` is the only file that imports the engine. No candidate earns that mechanism now.
- **The workload (folders, briefs, skills, supervisor): not a home.**
  - Each problem found here closes with plain code or content: a diff-conditional check, and a `kind` enum on findings.
  - Skill choice is between two skills, which is an `if`.
  - The supervisor's output is generation, which Jev does not do.
  - Ship or hold is the rule's core, and the state would be self-advocating text.
- **`apps/api`: the only plausible home, and only later.** Nothing at the board moves a run, so a wrong answer costs a person a glance. Nothing there costs a session either, so the ceiling is a person's minutes. If the probe passes, the shape is a suggestion asked once on a write path (`POST /api/runs`), never from a polled GET. The fact itself stays a person-written file that agent-workflows composes, so `wf decide` and the board agree. `apps/web` never calls TypeSafe: no key goes in a Vite bundle.

Jev's strengths are cheap typed reads of short text whose author has no stake. The project's money goes elsewhere: 450k-token resumed contexts, and rounds that the evidence says are earned (144 `fixed` against 7 `won't fix`). Jev's likeliest early use here is as a measuring instrument, not a component.
synthesis.sharedShape:
Only one candidate survives, so this is the shape any future one must take. It is described once, modelled on the check.

- **Who asks:** code, once, on an event that happens once: a run is started, or a review settles. Never inside a tick, never on a polled GET, never in `wf decide`. The inputs must be immutable records: a frozen brief, or a closeout on an ended attempt. They must be written by authors with no stake in the answer, and filtered in code first.
- **Two placements:**
  - If the run's own lifecycle raises the question, it is an engine task on a `HarnessSpec` that agent-workflows defines next to `CHECK` (`check.ts:117`). `runner.ts` files it under a deterministic task id, as `checkTaskId` does (`runner.ts:485`). The engine journals it once as filed, ended and settled.
  - If the board raises the question, one `apps/api` module writes `$WF_ROOT/judgments/<key>.json`. That module is the file's only writer.
- **What is recorded:**
  - the question text verbatim, the option list and a hash of the state;
  - the pinned model id `jev-1.13.0`, never an alias;
  - every probability, the confidence and the thresholds in force;
  - a recorded error when the call failed.
  
  A failure is a fact too. Without it a level-triggered pass would re-ask for ever. A model bump is a new key, not a re-ask.
- **Who reads it:** a person, as a label marked "suggested". Low confidence renders as "unsure" and sorts with the unhandled rows, so the failure direction is a re-read, never a hidden row. `assess`, `roundWanted`, `startQueued`, the gates and `wf decide`'s commands never read it. A person who confirms a suggestion writes their own fact file, in the `.cancelled` and asks pattern (`runner.ts:57`). agent-workflows composes that file on read.
- **Which package owns what:**
  - agent-workflows owns any harness and every person-fact file.
  - `apps/api` owns the SDK dependency and the key, if the consumer is the board.
  - The engine owns nothing.
  - `apps/web` only renders.
- **Tests:** each "never reads it" gets a test that makes it refuse, per CLAUDE.md.
synthesis.ruleWording:
The rule's reasons stand and nothing is adopted yet, so the line at `/home/yrnd1/projects/hkb-v2/docs/plan-hold-the-bar.md:973` could stay as it is. If the owner wants it to state its reason and leave room for a recorded judgment, I propose this wording:

"No model in a pass, and no model's answer on a control path. A tick, `assess`, `stepStatus`, `wf decide` and every gate are pure functions over records, and they call nothing that can answer differently twice. A model's typed answer may exist only as a recorded fact. It is asked once, by code, outside any pass. Its question, its pinned model version and its probabilities are journalled under a single writer. It is never re-asked for the same inputs. Such a fact may label or order what a person sees. It may never file, retry, round, start, approve, merge or hide anything. `roundWanted`, `startQueued`, the gates and `wf decide`'s commands do not read it. The inputs to such a question are records written by someone with no stake in the answer, never a step's account of its own work. The reviewer is a step, the decider is a person, and `wf` files nothing a person did not start. Still refused are an LLM judge of the work, an agent decider, auto-decomposition and auto-merge."

This keeps the letter. No pass asks, and no model's answer moves a run. It also names the three refusals explicitly. The one thing it admits is what the check already is: a fact recorded once. Add the wording only if and when the probe passes. Until then the rule stands unchanged.
synthesis.firstProbe:
The first probe is finding-to-brief matching, run offline outside the repository. It needs the owner's explicit say-so, because it sends briefs and findings to TypeSafe.

**Dataset.** I checked it by looking in `~/.agent-workflows`.
- `engine/tasks/*review*.jsonl` holds 142 files.
- 57 runs have a review closeout. All 57 last reviews say `again:false`.
- 40 of those carry findings: 60 findings and 48,045 characters of `what` text, about 800 characters each.
- `runs/*.json` holds 76 briefs, 257k characters in all.
- Five are leftovers briefs with 21 numbered items between them:
  - five-leftovers-from-the-revi-c0tl (5 items)
  - six-findings-the-last-review-6no7 (6)
  - four-leftovers-in-agent-work-3uyy (4)
  - four-leftovers-on-the-board-fmk9 (4)
  - two-findings-the-apps-lane-s-1qur (2)

**Labels.**
- **Negatives already exist and are exact.** A brief whose `createdAt` precedes the finding's review `ended` time cannot have taken the finding up. The roughly 70 ordinary briefs serve as decoys.
- **Positives do not exist yet.** I read the fmk9 brief. Its items restate the fix and do not name the source run, so each of the 21 items must be mapped by hand to a finding index. That is about an hour of work. No probe in this store has fully pre-made labels for a judgment that survived.

**Request shape.**
- One request per brief.
- `state` is that one run's `brief` string, exactly as it sits in `runs/<id>.json`.
- `questions` holds one noul per finding still open at that time, keyed `<run>#<i>`.
- Each noul reads, verbatim: "Does this request ask for the following problem to be fixed? Problem, in file <file>: <what>".
- The model is pinned to `jev-1.13.0`.
- Ask each pair a second time in a separate request, to measure determinism. The docs say nothing about it.
- Log the latency of every request.

**Metric.**
- Precision of "taken up" at the chosen high threshold, and recall over the 21 positives.
- The false-positive rate on the exact negatives (earlier briefs), reported separately.
- The flip rate between the two askings.
- p50 and p95 latency.

**Pass bar.**
- Precision at least 0.95 with recall at least 0.8.
- No earlier brief above threshold.
- Flips under 2% and none across a threshold.
- It must clearly beat a plain baseline of file-path plus backticked-symbol overlap.

Twenty-one positives can tune a threshold but cannot support a calibration claim, and the result should say so.

**Token cost at $0.042 per million input tokens.**
- 25 briefs: the 5 leftovers, 10 decoys and 10 earlier ones.
- Each is about 1.2k tokens of state plus 60 questions of about 220 tokens, roughly 14.5k tokens per request.
- That is about 360k tokens, or **$0.015**. Asked twice, it is about **$0.03**.
- If fan-out bills the state once per question, the total is about 2.1M tokens per asking, roughly $0.09 each, so under $0.20 for both. Requests would then split into batches of 20 to stay under the 64k limit.
- How fan-out is billed is unverified.

No survey examined CLAUDE.md itself as state. It holds about 30 'learned by the run' traps that are re-read every session. 'Which traps apply to this brief' is a fan-out of nouls over person-written text with no stake. Nobody counted whether selection would save tokens, or what a false 'does not apply' would cost.
The fates of open findings outside briefs were only sampled: hand commits such as 011bb03, and plan §6 notes. The true 'untracked' count is unknown.

Unrecounted claims:

A data-policy question nobody asked: which of TypeSafe's terms on retention and training apply to briefs and findings that are sent? The repository is private work.

The engine defect found along the way is unfiled. A `done` sighting with a schema and no closeout settles `succeeded`, and every task is filed with maxAttempts 1, so the nudge never runs. That cost three hand nudges and about $90 of sessions signed off late. It is worth more than any Jev candidate and belongs in `packages/agent-engine/docs/open-issues.md`.
risks: It adds a second vendor and a second secret. TYPESAFE_API_KEY would have to live in the api process or the daemon's environment. A Vite build inlines any `VITE_` variable, so the key must never reach `apps/web`.
The api makes no outbound call today. Its tests run hermetic, behind a fake `claude` on PATH, so a network dependency would need a fake of its own in `apps/api/test/harness.ts`.

It puts an outage or a rate limit in the path. A failed ask must be journalled as a fact, or a level-triggered reader re-asks on every pass or poll. Anything a person waits on (card write, run start) must not block on the call.

Latency and determinism are undocumented. An answer that flips across a threshold between two askings makes any judgment that is not journalled disagree with itself after a restart. So the mechanism allows only a recorded, once-asked answer.

Versions drift. The `jev-latest` and `jev-preview` aliases move. Thresholds tuned on `jev-1.13.0` are void on the next model. Pin the version, record it on every judgment, and treat a bump as a new key and a new tuning pass.

Data leaves the machine. Briefs, findings and possibly code excerpts from a private repository go to a third party. This needs the owner's explicit consent and a read of TypeSafe's retention terms. The probe must not be run by an unattended agent step.

State can be hostile or self-advocating, and Jev does not resist it. Closeouts and summaries are written by agents with a stake in passing. If a judgment ever reads them, the judged agent can steer it. The rule wording has to forbid such inputs, not just discourage them.

Usage drifts from label to gate. A recorded probability that sits beside `again` or the ship gate invites a later "ship if no behaviour leftovers". Each "never reads it" needs a test that makes it refuse. Otherwise the no-LLM rule erodes one convenience at a time.

The probabilities cannot be trusted per answer here. Calibration is claimed across groups of predictions, and the store offers 21 positives. Any threshold is tuned on too little, and per-answer probabilities shown to a person will read as more certain than they are.

It costs maintenance for a small payoff. An SDK, a harness or module, a record format, a staleness rule and a threshold-tuning chore would buy a person's minutes. By CLAUDE.md's own bar, that a tool earns its place when it replaces more code than it adds, none of the candidates qualifies today.
